pages.title: National population projections: 2024(base)–2078 | Stats NZ
passages: In the short term, the projections indicate:
* New Zealand’s population (5.29 million in 2024) has a 90 percent probability of increasing to between 5.36 and 5.62 million in 2028, and to between 5.46 and 5.86 million in 2031
* the population aged 65 years and over (65+, 0.87 million in 2024) has a 90 percent probability of increasing to between 0.99 and 1.00 million in 2028, and to between 1.07 and 1.09 million in 2031.
In the long term, the projections indicate:
* New Zealand’s population (5.29 million in 2024) has a 90 percent probability of increasing to between 6.12 and 7.21 million in 2051, and to between 6.61 and 9.05 million in 2078
* population growth will slow as New Zealand’s population ages and the gap between the number of births and deaths (natural increase) shrinks
These supersede the [2022-base projections](https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/national-population-projections-2022base2073/) released in July 2022.
The new projections have the provisional estimated resident population at 30 June 2024 as a base and cover the period 2025 to 2078 at one-year intervals.
Users can make their own judgement as to which projections are most suitable for their purposes.

At the time of release, the median projection (50th percentile) indicates an estimated 50 percent chance that the actual value will be lower and a 50 percent chance that the actual value will be higher than this percentile.
The median projection is not an assumed trajectory, but the median of the projection simulations, which vary every year around that median.
Other percentiles indicate the distribution of values (such as projection results or assumptions).
For example, the 25th percentile indicates an estimated 25 percent chance that the actual value will be lower and a 75 percent chance that the actual value will be higher than this percentile.
Shading in graphs indicates the chance that actual values will fall within a certain range.
The number of people aged 65+ doubled between 1997 and 2024 to reach 874,000.
Their number is projected to double again by around 2059.
There is an estimated 90 percent probability that there will be between 1.44 and 1.55 million people aged 65+ in 2051, and between 2.04 and 2.45 million in 2078.
Some of the largest growth occurs between 2012 and 2039 as the large birth cohorts of the 1950s, 1960s, and early 1970s move into the 65+ age group.

The base population is 5.290 million (provisional) at 30 June 2024 ([National population estimates: At 31 March 2025 (2023-base)](https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/national-population-estimates-at-31-march-2025-2023-base/)).
This is 110,800 (2.1 percent) higher than the 2022-base median projection for 2024.
New Zealand’s base population as at 30 June 2024 is 5.290 million (provisional).
It incorporates results from the 2023 Census of Population and Dwellings and the 2023 Post-enumeration Survey (a sample survey to measure census coverage).

[Estimated resident population (2023-base): At 30 June 2023](https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/estimated-resident-population-2023-base-at-30-june-2023/) and [Estimated resident population 2023: Data sources and methods](https://www.stats.govt.nz/methods/estimated-resident-population-2023-data-sources-and-methods/) has more information about the base population.
The estimated resident population (ERP) is the best available measure of the number of people usually living in New Zealand.
The ERP at 30 June 2023 includes estimates of uncertainty from contributing data and estimation processes, where possible.
The main source of uncertainty in the ERP was the estimated net census undercount measured by the 2023 Post-enumeration Survey.
However, the estimation did not incorporate uncertainty around data quality in individual sources or from adjustments made to the ERP at 30 June 2023.

* Adjustments in deriving population estimates: This includes the adjustments applied in deriving the ERP at 30 June of the census year (for example, net census undercount). It also includes uncertainty associated with the post-censal components of population change (births, deaths, and net migration between the census date and 30 June).

* Migration estimates for more recent months have greater uncertainty and are therefore subject to larger revisions than estimates for earlier periods. Estimated net migration is a gain of 70,400 (provisional) for the June year 2024 (based on estimates published in May 2025). These estimates could be revised up or down, before final estimates are published in December 2025. See [International migration](https://www.stats.govt.nz/publications/?dateFiltersID=67&filters=Information%20releases%2CInternational%20migration) releases for more details.
Simulations of the base population are produced by drawing a random number sampled from a normal distribution with a mean of zero.
The fan chart shows the total population living in New Zealand from 1953 to 2078.
The total New Zealand population is estimated from 1953 to 2024 and projected from 2025 to 2078.
A black line represents the median (50th percentile).
The dark shaded area represents the 50 percent range between the 25th and 75th percentiles.
There is an estimated 50 percent chance that the total New Zealand population will fall within this dark shaded area.
The light shaded area below and above the dark shaded area represents the range between 5th and 25th percentiles, and between the 75th and 95th percentiles.
There is an estimated 90 percent chance that the total New Zealand population will fall within the light and dark shaded areas.

pages.title: Population growth continues to taper
passages: Our take on the latest **National population estimates** (Wed 20 Nov 2024)
Population growth slows to 1.2%pa in September 2024 quarter
Net migration eases to 44,900 for year ending September 2024

* New Zealand’s resident population grew 1.2%pa in the September 2024 quarter to an estimated total of 5,348,600. Stats NZ have continued to revise down their population estimates, with the June 2024 population 5,100 lower than previously estimated.

* Annual net migration fell from 68,500 in the year to June 2024 to 44,900 in the year to September 2024. Net migration in the September 2024 quarter was less than a third of net migration in September 2023 quarter, which was one of New Zealand’s highest quarters on record

* With net migration slowing, growth in the under-65-year-old population has slowed sharply. The under 15-year-old population grew just 0.4%pa the September 2024 quarter, dragged down by a 0.7% decline in the 0-4-year-old population. The working age 15–64-year-old population rose 1.1%pa, but there was a 1.8% fall in the 25-29-year-old age group.
* The 65-years-and-older population rose 2.9%pa, with the strongest growth occurring in the 75-79-year-old population, up 4.9%pa.

* Growth in the number of dwellings continues to slow, up 1.6%pa in the September 2024 quarter, down from a peak of 2.3%pa in the June 2023 quarter. Dwelling growth is at its lowest level since September 2019.
### Population growth slows sharply in under-65s

* New Zealand’s population growth continues to slow down from a record high, with growth of 1.2%pa in the September 2024 quarter back into normal territory. The last time New Zealand’s population grew at around 1.2%, before the pandemic, was in 2013.

* Annual net migration is moderating, and we expect it to continue trending down, driven by further falls in non-citizen arrivals. Non-citizen arrivals are still at historically elevated levels, with 36,700 arriving in the September 2024 quarter alone, despite New Zealand’s weak labour market and rising unemployment rate.

* It is unsurprising to see the over-65 age group leading our population growth, particularly as the net migration injection into younger age groups has pulled back as more young people leave New Zealand, and fewer arrive to chase fewer job opportunities. However, it is concerning to see such weak growth in the under 15-year-old age group, which is in effect the future working age population. This slow under-15s growth isn’t a problem right now, but may become a constraint for employment growth as economic activity picks up in coming years.
